title: ENDING EVERY TYPESCRIPT DEBATE in 90 minutes
summary: Matt Pocock hosts a 'Supreme Court of TypeScript' live stream, dressed in a suit and wielding a gavel, where he argues both sides of the four most divisive TypeScript debates and then issues verdicts voted on by the live chat. The court hears four cases: enums versus string unions (verdict: don't use enums), types versus interfaces as your default object declaration (verdict: it depends - use whatever your team uses), whether to ban explicit any via an ESLint rule (verdict: ban it in application code with escape hatches, allow it in library code and test suites), and whether to force explicit function return types (verdict: don't force it - the more consumers a function has, the more a return type pays off). Between cases he rules on side motions: namespaces are obsolete, TypeScript will eventually be superseded but typed development is never going away, and migrations should go file-by-file at maximum strictness starting at the top of the dependency tree.
what_you_learn: You get decision-ready rulings on the four TS debates every team wastes time re-arguing, plus the reasoning behind each: structural typing (why nominal enums fight the language), declaration merging, dependency-tree thinking for where type strictness matters most, and how to configure lint rules so juniors get consistent feedback without losing escape hatches. Even as a Java/Python-leaning backend dev, the structural-vs-nomental framing and 'types exist to power tooling, not to make JS safe' mental model transfer directly to how you read and design typed APIs.

skills.name: TypeScript Type System
skills.description: Migrate to TypeScript file-by-file at the highest strictness you can manage, starting at the top of the dependency tree, instead of one big strict-false PR.

skills.name: Software Architecture
skills.description: Typing mistakes in leaf code are cheap; an any or bad generic high in the tree in your utils folder silently degrades every file below it.

skills.name: Package & Build Tooling
skills.description: no-explicit-any as an error in application code, disabled in libraries and tests, with eslint-disable-next-line as the auditable escape hatch.

skills.name: TypeScript Compiler Performance
skills.description: TSC and TS Server type-check faster with interfaces over deep intersections, per the TypeScript performance wiki - mostly a library-author concern.

learnings.title: Verdict on enums: don't use them - they break structural typing
learnings.detail: The case for enums: a single source of truth for values (LogLevel.Debug), easy renames via go-to-references, and parity with enums in databases like Postgres. The case against: you must import the enum everywhere, and two enums with identical members are not mutually assignable - LogLevel2.Debug cannot be passed where LogLevel.Debug is expected, which breaks TypeScript's structural type system (shapes matter, not names). Daniel Rosenwasser, the TS program manager, has said enums would not make it into the language if proposed today. The chat-voted verdict: don't use them.

learnings.title: The as const object is the modern enum replacement
learnings.detail: The preferred alternative is export const shapes = { circle: 'circle', square: 'square' } as const plus export type Shapes = keyof typeof shapes. Callers pass plain literal values with no import, autocomplete still works, and unlike enums the pattern can map to richer data structures - e.g. a record keyed by shape name whose values are coordinate objects - which produces genuinely useful generic mappings. Verdict: string unions are the natural product of a structural type system; enums are a type-system dead end.

learnings.title: Never export enums from a library
learnings.detail: A recurring side-ruling: exporting enums from library code is a pain for consumers, who must import your enum just to pass a string argument. It is also cruel to JavaScript consumers, since TypeScript libraries compile down to JS where the enum construct does not exist. Library APIs should accept literal values so plain JS callers can use them.

learnings.title: Verdict on types vs interfaces: it depends - default to whatever your team uses
learnings.detail: Hats argued for types: duplicate declarations are errors, matching JavaScript semantics; you don't realize interfaces silently declaration-merge when you declare the same name twice in one scope (with a safeguard: merged members of the same property must keep the same type). No-hats argued for interfaces: cleaner OOP feel with class Foo implements and extends, intersections of object types can silently produce never (ID: string & number), and interfaces type-check faster. The judge ruled the performance argument mostly moot for apps, called it a hung jury, and the verdict is: pick your team's default and stop debating it.

learnings.title: Declaration merging is the one place interfaces are genuinely needed
learnings.detail: Interfaces exist for a real reason: augmenting globals. Declaring interface Window { foo: string } in your project merges with the built-in Window type, and window.foo becomes typed - this is how libraries add things to the global scope. But that same power means every casual interface declaration carries a feature you probably didn't ask for; types behave exactly like JavaScript duplicate-identifier semantics with no excess baggage.

learnings.title: An any leaks downstream and disables every type check it touches
learnings.detail: Demonstrated with a pick-from-object helper: writing obj as any inside it made the returned object any too, killing autocomplete for callers - an any high in your dependency tree wrecks every file beneath it. Matt's diagnosis of most bad TypeScript projects: not enough generics, too many anys. unknown is no substitute here because it serves a different purpose - unknown keeps type checking on and forces narrowing, while any turns checking off entirely.

learnings.title: Verdict on any: disallow it in application code, allow it in libraries and tests
learnings.detail: The ruling has three parts. In application code enable the ESLint no-explicit-any rule so juniors get consistent feedback, and let developers opt out explicitly with eslint-disable-next-line, which surfaces in code review as an auditable 'I could not find a better way' marker. In library code, any is legitimate - generic libraries describe gnarly JS and need escape hatches, backed by unit tests. In test suites, type safety barely matters because tests are themselves the safety, so strict-false should be the default in your tests folder. He also confesses he once papered over a real bug (of instead of in) with as any, which a lint rule would have forced him to fix.

learnings.title: no-unsafe-any is the rule that catches anys as they propagate
learnings.detail: Mentioned during the any case: typescript-eslint's no-unsafe-* family uses TS Server to detect anys flowing through your codebase, warning when an unsafe any propagates instead of banning any outright. It is slow and costly in performance, but it gives you the safety without the restrictiveness - a good middle ground if a blanket ban feels too harsh. Matt's related taste: he hates warnings that don't fail the build - make it an error or don't bother.

learnings.title: Verdict on return types: don't force them - benefit scales with consumer count
learnings.detail: The case for forcing explicit return types: you can't know how many consumers a function will have, explicit annotations move errors closer to the function, and they make the contract readable in code review without an IDE. The case against: most application code is leaf nodes consumed only by a framework (why annotate JSX.Element on a React component?), and explicit annotations can lie - a leftover string | number annotation on a function that now only returns strings. Inference is always the most correct answer because it is pulled from the code itself. Verdict: forcing return types by default is garbage; the more consumers a function has (utils folders, libraries), the more an annotation pays off.

learnings.title: TypeScript exists to power tooling, and it will die by supersession not disappearance
learnings.detail: Asked 'will TypeScript die?', Matt argues TS exists not to make JavaScript type-safe (impossible - escape hatches everywhere) but to power tooling: autocomplete, refactors, and even JavaScript IntelliSense in VS Code via TS Server. He doesn't think types will ever be understood by V8 or the browser; instead the types-as-comments proposal opens a syntactic space in JS where any type system can live, so TS may eventually be superseded by something faster or more ergonomic. But we're never going back to plain .js files - the cat is out of the bag. Side ruling: namespaces are a pre-modules hack with no remaining use case beyond scoping globals; Rob Palmer of TC39 'would not mind if namespaces went away'.

learnings.title: Migrate file-by-file at max strictness, starting at the top of the dependency tree
learnings.detail: The anti-pattern: one giant PR converting everything to TS with strict: false in tsconfig - CI stays green but you defer all type errors to one brutal upgrade later. The recommended path, which Matt credits to Mark Erikson: start with the files highest in the dependency tree (utils, reusable abstractions), at the highest strictness you can manage, then work down; by the time you reach the leaves you get automatic inference for free. You accept living with a codebase that's half JavaScript for a while - that is the sensible price.

learnings.title: Strict mode is not optional, and other cases the court refused to hear
learnings.detail: On strict mode Matt is absolute: the only real choice these days is strict on - strict: false is not an option worth debating. Cases denied a hearing: import vs import type ('doesn't make enough difference'), naming conventions for single-letter generics (deserves renaming TFunc/TResult, but not a court case), namespaces (always a nay), interface file names starting with I ('absolutely not'), and default exports vs named exports (belongs in the High Court of JavaScript). Pattern takeaway: genuinely debatable topics have real trade-offs on both sides; syntactical preferences don't.

key_points: Verdict 1 - enums: don't use them; string unions are the structural-typing-native choice.
Verdict 2 - types vs interfaces: it depends; use whatever your team already uses.
Verdict 3 - any: ban it in application code with eslint-disable escape hatches, allow it in libraries and tests.
Verdict 4 - return types: never force them; the more consumers, the more an annotation pays.
Two enums with identical members can't be compared - that breaks structural typing.
An any in your utils folder wrecks type safety in every file below it in the dependency tree.
TypeScript exists to power tooling, not to make JavaScript type-safe.
Migrate file-by-file at max strictness from the top of the dependency tree - never one big strict-false PR.
Tests are themselves the safety, so strict-false is the right default in test suites.
